Beethoven privacy statement

Save a copy. Press Ctrl+S (⌘S on a Mac) to keep this page as a file, or print it to PDF. This is version 11; it is part of the Trial Edition License Agreement.

Version 11, 2026-10-04. Part of the Beethoven Trial Edition License Agreement (LICENSE.txt) and of any Full Edition agreement that names it. You can save and print this text; it is also at https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/privacy.html.

Who collects: Gregory Schwing, trading as OpenSpineConsortium (“Licensor”), the maintainer of Beethoven. Questions and requests: the notice address on the support page at https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/support.html. Beethoven is licensed to individuals; it is not provided by or on behalf of any school, and Licensor is not acting for one.

Beethoven is a browser extension that starts, watches and stops a job in your own cluster account, over a secure shell (ssh) connection to your cluster’s login node (the ssh path, which it tries first) or through your university’s Open OnDemand portal (the portal path); a small helper program, the Bridge, that ships inside the extension and that you may install on your computer to carry the ssh connection; and a set of scripts (the framework) that runs in your cluster account. The job runs Claude Code, which you signed in to yourself. This statement says what stays in your browser, what the Bridge does on your computer, what happens when you sign in to your cluster over ssh, what goes to your cluster account, what your university sees on the ssh path, what your portal sees, what happens when you sign in to Claude and when the portal’s shell asks for your password, what Anthropic receives, what Licensor receives, and what is never collected. The ssh path and the Bridge came with Beethoven 12.0.0; they have been tried mostly against ssh servers Licensor ran itself, set up like your university’s, and have had little use yet with real accounts on a real cluster. The signed installers of the Bridge for Windows and macOS, new in Beethoven 15.0.0, have not yet been opened on a real Windows computer or Mac.

The one durable secret in the extension’s storage is the browser’s key for the ssh path (above), whose line in your cluster account lets it run only the gate described below; there is no key of Licensor’s, and your own sign-in to your cluster identifies you. The one-time step of the portal path, below, makes a key in your cluster account, never in your browser. The extension never reads your portal’s sign-in: your browser attaches the sign-in it holds (a cookie, or the sign-in it keeps after you type into its own box) to requests to that one website, the extension’s own background requests included, until the browser closes. Before you agree to the terms, the extension sends nothing anywhere. After you agree, it opens a connection to your cluster’s ssh port, through the Bridge, only to check that it can reach your cluster, to sign in, or to do what you pressed; and it asks your portal’s address whether it answers, with requests that carry no sign-in or cookie and from which it learns only whether an answer came: once when you agree, every three seconds while it waits for you to turn on your VPN (GlobalProtect at Wayne State), and when you press Try again. The one thing it reads about you from the portal is the account name the portal’s own dashboard page shows for your session. On the ssh path your account name is the one you type into the sign-in sheet, and it counts only once your cluster has accepted the sign-in made with it. The extension never reads, stores, copies or relays a Claude credential: Claude Code keeps its own sign-in in your cluster account, and the framework reads only Claude Code’s own report of whether it is signed in, with the account and plan that report names. The extension writes to your clipboard only when you press a Copy button and when you open the portal’s terminal for the one-time step below, to put its one line there; it never reads your clipboard. The QR codes are drawn on your device: your session’s link, for your phone, and, on the welcome page, under What you need and on the phone route below, the addresses of your university’s instructions and of the app stores’ pages for GlobalProtect and Google Authenticator, each printed under its code; the tour is drawn from files in the extension’s package. Nothing is fetched or sent to show them.

The Bridge on your computer

The ssh path needs a program on your computer, because a browser extension cannot open an ssh connection itself. The Bridge, which the extension’s screens call the helper, is that program. It ships inside the extension’s package, and the extension offers its installer from there: nothing is downloaded from Licensor or anyone else. You save the installer and open it once, in your own user account; it needs no administrator rights. What the Bridge is depends on your system:

  • On Windows and on a Mac, the Bridge is a compiled program of Licensor’s (written in Rust, with no code of anyone else’s but the Rust standard library and the start-up and runtime support code its compiler links in, which THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md lists), and its installer is a signed package. On Windows it is a Windows Installer file (beethoven-bridge-windows.msi) signed by Licensor; it installs into your own account, and Windows’ Settings list it afterwards, under Apps, as “Beethoven bridge”. On a Mac it is an installer package (beethoven-bridge-mac.pkg) signed by Licensor and notarized by Apple (checked by Apple’s automated service before it was offered); it installs into your own home folder only.
  • On Linux, the Bridge is a script run by Perl, or by Python 3 where Perl is absent; these come with your system. Its installer is a script in a zip file.
  • A Bridge you installed from a zip file with Beethoven 14.0.0 or earlier keeps working until you remove it: a script, run by Windows PowerShell on Windows or by Perl on a Mac, not signed and not listed under Apps; the uninstaller placed beside it removes it. On Windows it uses the same folder as the signed installer, so Beethoven’s settings ask you to remove it before you install that one.

When you open a signed installer, your Mac or your Windows computer may check the installer’s signature with Apple or Microsoft, as it does for any signed program it is asked to open. That check is your system’s own behaviour, between your computer and them, and it tells Licensor nothing.

Each installer puts the Bridge’s few files in a folder of your user account and registers it with Chrome, and with the other browsers built on Chromium that it finds, so that the browser knows where it is (on Windows a key in your own part of the registry, for Chrome and for Microsoft Edge; on a Mac or on Linux a small file in the browser’s folder in your home folder); the registration names Beethoven as the only extension that may start it (the signed installers name the Beethoven of the Chrome Web Store, written into them when they are built). Chrome starts the Bridge when the extension asks for it, and the Bridge ends when the extension lets it go. The Bridge opens a network connection only to your cluster’s ssh port (at Wayne State, grid.wayne.edu, port 22, which is written into the Bridge; another address only if a settings file placed beside it names one, and the installers in the package bring none) and carries bytes between the extension and that port. What it carries is the ssh connection, which is encrypted between the extension and your cluster: the Bridge does not read it, keep it or log it, holds no password, key or other credential, offers no shell, runs no other program and sends nothing to Licensor. On Windows, Settings, Apps, “Beethoven bridge”, Uninstall removes its files and the registration; on a Mac and on Linux, and for a Bridge installed from a zip file with Beethoven 14.0.0 or earlier, the uninstaller placed beside it does. If you do not install the Bridge, the extension uses the portal path.

When you sign in to your cluster over ssh

The first time you use the ssh path in this browser, the extension asks you to sign in on its own sign-in sheet, a page of the extension: your account name (your AccessID at Wayne State), your cluster password, and the one-time verification code from Google Authenticator that your university’s cluster asks for. The extension opens the ssh connection through the Bridge, checks that the server’s identity (its host key) is the one your university’s site profile names, and stops without sending anything about you if it is not. It then sends your account name, your password and your code to your cluster inside the encrypted connection, as the cluster asks for them, and to nobody else. The password and code are not kept: they stay in the browser’s memory only until they are sent, and are dropped then (a browser cannot promise when its memory is overwritten); they are not kept in any storage, not written to the audit log or to Show log, not sent to Licensor or anyone else, and the sheet never offers to remember them. The extension never makes a verification code and never sees the secret your authenticator app keeps.

In that same sign-in the extension makes the browser’s key (see the table above) and runs one command in your account, the lab’s framework’s browser-key step, which adds the key’s line there (see What goes to your own cluster account). The connection you signed in to with your password and code stays open, in the browser’s memory only, for up to ten minutes after setup, so that your first Connect can run the Claude sign-in in it without asking for your password and code again; it closes when that sign-in ends, when the ten minutes pass, when you cancel, or when the browser closes. From then on this browser signs in with the key and asks you for nothing, and your cluster knows those connections by the key, not by your password. Protecting the key with a passkey is your choice and off unless you turn it on, on the sign-in sheet, on the screen that offers it once after setup, or in Settings: then the extension asks Windows Hello or Touch ID (or your device’s PIN or password) to unlock the key once each time you open the browser, and keeps what unlocks it only in the browser’s memory until the browser closes. You can turn it off again in Settings. If your lab sets a number of days for the key’s line, the extension asks you to sign in with your password and code again once the line has lapsed, and it asks the same whenever the key is missing or refused.

If your cluster refuses a code with its message that may mean a mistyped code or no verification code set up, the extension asks you which; if you say you have none, it shows two ways to set one up: on your computer, or on your phone. Both use your university’s own pages and its 2FA Setup app, which you run yourself, with your university’s VPN; the extension takes no part in them and sees nothing of them. The phone route shows QR codes drawn on your device, for the app stores’ pages of GlobalProtect and Google Authenticator and for your university’s instructions for Google Authenticator on the grid, with each address printed under its code (the welcome page and What you need also show one for its instructions for GlobalProtect); scanning one opens that page on your phone, which its website sees as it sees any visit. On the computer route, Open the grid’s website opens your portal in a new tab, as a link would; the extension runs nothing there. Before any step that could lead you to run 2FA Setup a second time, the extension warns you that running it replaces the code you already have.

The Claude sign-in (see What happens when you sign in to Claude) runs only in a connection you signed in to with your password and code, or through your portal, never through the browser’s key.

Forget this computer, in Settings, deletes the key from your browser and asks your cluster, through the gate, to remove the key’s line. If your cluster cannot be reached, or the key is protected and you do not unlock it, the extension says so, and the line stays until it is removed, which hpcworker browser-key remove, run in a terminal on the cluster, does. A passkey you made is kept by your system or your browser’s password manager: the extension asks it to drop the passkey, and where it does not, you delete it there.

Relays and the pilot app

Beethoven can carry the ssh path through a relay server instead of the Bridge, but only through one your university’s site profile names. None is named in this version, and none is used. If one is ever named, this statement will first say who runs it and what it sees: a relay would see the encrypted connection, your network address and the times, never your password, your code or anything inside the connection.

A pilot edition of Beethoven made as an installable web app (an Isolated Web App) can reach the grid over ssh without the Bridge. It is given only to a student who asks for it, by the lab lead, as a file the student installs after turning on two of Chrome’s developer settings, which make Chrome show a warning at every start. It keeps and sends what this statement says the extension keeps and sends; anything it does differently will be written here before it is given to anyone.

What goes to your own cluster account

The framework’s settings, the job files, a random per-job token in a file only you can read, the job’s status files, and a plain-words progress log for each worker (when it was asked for, got a computer, came online with its claude.ai link, renewed itself or stopped). The framework’s scripts are not copied into your account: they stay in the one shared copy your university’s lab keeps on the cluster, and a small launcher that runs that copy, and a one-line note of where that copy is, take their place. The install also adds a marked block of a few lines to ~/.bashrc so that a terminal finds the tool. Nothing about your approval goes there. When you tick the statement in the panel and press Connect, the framework writes one small file in your account, through the portal’s shell or, on the ssh path, through the gate (its own marker, ~/.hpcworker/consent), one line: the word yes, the time, and the random installation identifier from your browser. Your worker gives that answer to Claude Code when Claude Code asks its one-time question “Enable Remote Control?”, and after the first session Claude Code’s own record of your answer takes over. If your portal’s shell asks for your password, the one-time step below adds three things in your account’s ~/.ssh folder: a key of its own (beethoven_ed25519 and its public half), a marked block in ~/.ssh/config that has ssh offer that key first when the portal’s shell connects you to the login node, and one line in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys that lets that key in only from the address the terminal came from, which at your institution is its Open OnDemand server; it makes ~/.ssh and authorized_keys readable by you alone, as ssh requires, leaves your own keys and lines as they are, and refuses to change a file there that is a link to another file. That key is a file in your own account, protected as your other files are; anyone who obtained it and could connect from that server could use it, so the framework hides it from Claude Code inside your worker. Mark this workspace restricted writes a small marker file in that workspace. While Connect runs, the framework keeps the last line of the sign-in sitting (with the account and plan Claude Code names) in a file only you can read under ~/.hpcworker/log, and removes it when Connect ends; it also leaves a marker in your worker’s folder when a sign-in starts, so that a worker waiting for that sign-in does not give up on you while you are on Anthropic’s page. Everything there is in your own account under your institution’s rules; Licensor has no access to it.

On the ssh path, the first sign-in’s browser-key step adds one line to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, makes ~/.ssh readable by you alone if it has to create it, keeps the file’s previous contents, without any line of Beethoven’s, as ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.beethoven-prev, refuses to change a file there that is a link or that others can change, and leaves your own keys and lines as they are. The line holds restrict, the command hpcworker gate from the lab’s shared copy, the public half of the browser’s key, the tag beethoven-browser and the date it was added. restrict takes away a terminal, forwarding and file transfer, and the command means that whatever the key asks for, the gate runs instead. The gate does only this, each a short command on the login node: report the framework’s version, your account name and whether Claude Code says you are signed in; start your worker, always without any Claude sign-in; report your worker’s state; read four of your worker’s own files (its status, its connection, its node and its progress log); stop it; mark its workspace restricted; and remove the line. It refuses anything else, and it allows at most three worker names in any seven days (your own sign-in with your password and code clears them), twelve starts or new restrictions in any hour, and two watches at once, which it counts in a small file in your account’s state folder on the cluster (the worker names and when each was last used, and the times of the last hour’s starts). The line stays until you or the gate remove it: withdrawing your approval does not remove it. Your account keeps one such line: signing in over ssh from another browser replaces it. If your lab sets a number of days for it, the gate removes the line once it is older.

What your university sees on the ssh path

Your university’s login node records each ssh connection as it records any other: the time, the network address it came from (your computer’s own, with no VPN), your account, and whether it signed in with a password and code or with a key. Your network and your university’s see a connection to the cluster’s ssh port. On the ssh path your worker is started, watched and stopped without your portal: the extension asks your portal only whether it answers (see What stays in your browser), with requests that carry no sign-in.

What your portal sees

On the portal path, the extension makes requests to your university’s Open OnDemand portal, and only to it, using the sign-in your browser already holds, from the extension’s own background, with no portal tab where your browser allows it: waking the portal’s own web server up if it is asleep; reading the dashboard (when the panel opens, on each press that needs the grid, and about once a minute while the panel is open; every two seconds while you sign in); listing and reading your worker’s files through the portal’s Files app (every five seconds while a worker starts and the panel is open, every thirty seconds while it starts and the panel is closed, and about once a minute otherwise), and reading the version number of your lab’s shared copy of the framework; and opening the shell for one command at a time (setting your account up to use the lab’s copy; connect, which starts your worker and, when needed, holds the sign-in sitting described below; status, about once a minute while your worker waits for a computer and the panel is open; stop; and mark restricted), once after your first sign-in to test how the portal’s shell can be reached (opened and closed with nothing typed but exit), during the one-time step below to test whether the shell still asks for a password, and, from Details, for the checks and the check job you start there. The extension types into the shell only once the shell has shown it is ready (its prompt), never at a password prompt. A shell connection from the extension’s background arrives with the extension’s own origin (chrome-extension://...) in the portal’s logs. Your institution’s logs record those requests as they record any use of the portal; the shell’s page token appears in the portal’s access log, as it does when you open the shell yourself. The extension opens the portal in a tab only for you to sign in there (in your browser’s own sign-in box, or on the portal’s own sign-in page), never sees what you type there, and closes that tab; where your portal does not share its sign-in with the extension, it opens a background tab for one action and closes it. It also opens the portal’s own terminal page in a tab for the one-time step below, and your worker’s folder in the portal’s Files app when you press Your files. The extension never signs in for you and never touches a multi-factor step. It reads no other website and makes no request to claude.ai. When it opens a claude.ai page (your session’s link when a worker you started is ready, Open my session and New session, or the connectors page from the optional step) or Anthropic’s sign-in page, it opens it in a new browser tab, as a bookmark would, and runs nothing there; it closes Anthropic’s sign-in tab once you are signed in, and Open my session may bring forward the claude.ai tab it opened itself.

What happens when you sign in to Claude

Claude Code itself does the sign-in, inside your job’s container on a compute node, through Anthropic’s own paste-code flow. When Claude Code on your cluster already reports you signed in, no sitting runs. Otherwise the extension starts that sitting for you, in the same command that starts your worker, through the portal’s shell or, on the ssh path, through a connection you signed in to with your password and code (never with the browser’s key, which the gate refuses for this), reads the short lines the framework prints (that your account is set up, that your Remote Control answer is recorded, that your worker is in line, with its job number and folder, that the sitting is running and still waiting, the address of Anthropic’s sign-in page, that it is waiting for the code, and Claude Code’s own report afterwards with the account and plan it names), opens the sign-in page in a new tab, and shows you one box. Claude Code’s own screen is never sent to your browser: it stays in a temporary file on the compute node that only you can read and that is removed when the sitting ends. You sign in on Anthropic’s page with your own account, click Authorize, and paste the code the page shows into that box. The extension types the code once into the sitting on your cluster, through the same connection, and then forgets it: the code is not kept in any storage, not written to the audit log (which records only how many bytes were typed) and not sent to Licensor or anywhere else; on the compute node it is passed to Claude Code without being echoed. The extension never reads the sign-in page, never reads your clipboard, and never sees the credential Claude Code makes from the code; that credential stays in Claude Code’s own folder in your cluster account. The extension closes the sign-in tab it opened once Claude Code reports you are signed in, unless that tab has loaded another page since you pasted the code. The sitting ends by itself within ten minutes of starting on the compute node, and the wait for a compute node is bounded too (the extension closes the connection after fifteen minutes at the latest); if it ends without a sign-in, nothing is kept and you can start it again.

When the portal’s shell asks for your password (the portal path)

An account with no key on the cluster may find that the portal’s shell asks for a password when the extension opens it. The extension never types a password: it stops before typing anything and, when you next press a button that needs the grid, asks you, once, to open the portal’s own terminal page. When you press Open the grid terminal, it opens that page (the portal’s Shell app) in a tab beside the panel and puts one line on your clipboard. You type your password there yourself, into your institution’s own page; the extension never sees it. On that page the extension’s page script watches only the page’s title, to tell when your shell is up: it listens to no keys, reads nothing the terminal shows and stores nothing from the page. When you press I’m in, or the title shows that your shell is up, it types the one line into the terminal for you; where it cannot, you paste it. The line runs hpcworker login-setup from your lab’s shared copy, in your own account: it makes a key there, lets that key into your account only from the computer the terminal came from, which at your institution is its Open OnDemand server, and has ssh offer it when the portal’s shell connects you (see What goes to your own cluster account). It never reads, changes or prints a key you already have, and never prints a private key. The key never leaves your cluster account: the extension does not see it, keeps nothing about it in your browser and sends nothing about it to anyone; it keeps only which tab it opened, until the browser closes, and whether the shell still asks for a password (see the table above). It then checks whether the shell opens without a password, every two seconds for ten seconds and then every ten seconds for up to five minutes; each check opens the portal’s shell once and closes it, which the login node records as a sign-in that stopped at the password prompt. It closes the terminal tab it opened once the shell opens without a password, and carries on with what you pressed. If the computer the terminal comes from changes, the shell asks again and the step is offered again. hpcworker login-setup --remove, run in a terminal on the cluster, removes the key and both entries. This step came with Beethoven 11.0.0 and has been tried only against the lab’s mock portal, not yet on a real cluster by an account without a key.

What Anthropic receives

Through Claude Code, which you signed in to with your own account: your prompts, the files the worker reads, every command’s output, and the title your worker’s session shows in claude.ai (at Wayne State, “Wayne State grid”). While you are connected through claude.ai or the Claude app, the session transcript, including your messages, Claude’s responses and tool activity, is also stored on Anthropic’s servers. On a personal plan Anthropic retains it five years if you have model training on and 30 days otherwise. No BAA covers a personal plan. Remote Control usage draws from your plan’s shared limit. Anthropic’s terms and privacy policy apply to that data, not this statement. The extension shows these facts in short form before your first worker starts, with the full text one click away, and a one-line reminder beside Connect each time you start one.

What Licensor receives

From the extension: the approval check, and two small files. The extension makes no request to Licensor before you have accepted the agreement. After that:

  • The approval check. Once your cluster has accepted your sign-in and the extension knows your account name, it asks Licensor’s access service whether that account is approved: when you first sign in to your cluster after you agree, about once a day while it is in use, and again when you open the panel after a day has passed or after a no. The request is sent without cookies, over an encrypted connection, to the address named in the services file below (Licensor’s access service, https://beethoven-access.openspineconsortium.workers.dev), and carries: the account name your cluster accepted for your sign-in (the one your portal’s dashboard shows, or, on the ssh path, the one you typed into the sign-in sheet, sent only after your cluster accepted the sign-in made with it, or the one your cluster reports for a sign-in with the browser’s key), your portal’s hostname (on the ssh path, the hostname of the portal your university’s site profile names), the product name (bridge), the extension’s version and the random installation identifier described above; like any request, it arrives at a time. The service answers yes or no, and nothing else about you or anyone else. A no may carry one of three reasons: that your account is already set up on another installation (the panel then says so and offers no button: your lab lead moves the approval), that this installation is already set up for another account (the panel says so and offers no button: your lab lead releases it), or that this version is too old (the panel asks you to install the current one from the lab’s private listing). The extension keeps a yes for up to a day, and for up to seven days when the service cannot be reached, so an outage on Licensor’s side does not stop your work; it keeps a no for ten minutes, and while the answer is no it starts no worker and, unless the reason is one of those three, offers you a button to ask for access.
  • Two files, once a day. https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/services.json (the address of the access service) and https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/killlist.json (the signed list of withdrawn extension versions). Both requests are sent without cookies and carry nothing about you beyond what any web request carries (your network address, which the web host’s ordinary server logs may record for a short time); the files hold addresses and the list only.

Those are the only requests the extension ever makes to Licensor. In particular:

  • there is no key of Licensor’s and no activation step; your institution’s own sign-in identifies you; the extension never reads your portal’s sign-in, cookie or password, and the cluster password and code you type into its sign-in sheet go only to your cluster;
  • the extension sends no error reports, no crash reports and no usage data; it has no code for them and no address to send them to;
  • your acceptance record, your statements, your audit log, your activity list, your settings, the browser’s key and what the extension remembers about your worker stay in your browser, and the Bridge sends nothing to Licensor.

What Licensor records from the checks. One record for each account and product: the account name, the product, and the portal hostname and the version of the latest check; when the account was first and last checked; how many checks there have been; the answer of the latest check and, with a no, the reason the service gave, if any (another installation, another account, a version too old); when the answer last changed; and a salted hash of the network address of the latest check (the address itself is not kept). The service also counts each day’s checks per account and per hashed address, to limit them, and deletes those counts after two days. This record sits with your access record.

One approved account, one installation. The first installation that asks about an approved account is bound to it: the service keeps that installation’s identifier with the product, the version and the times it first and last asked, and, for that identifier, the account it is bound to. A check for the same account from any other installation (another computer, another browser profile, a reinstallation) is refused, and so is a check from that installation for any other account; the service counts such refusals and keeps the times of the first and the last one and the first eight characters of a one-way hash of the refused installation’s identifier. When another installation asks about an account, the service e-mails Licensor, at most once a day per account, with a link that can move the approval to that installation, so that Licensor can move it or withdraw it. The identifier is random: it is not read from your device or derived from it, and Licensor cannot tell from it which computer it is on. One account is the exception: the account the store’s reviewers use with the lab’s mock portal (st1234) is approved only in a check whose portal is on the reviewer’s own computer (localhost), from any installation, and binds none; from any other portal it is answered as an unknown account is, and nothing is bound or e-mailed. The Bridge on the same computer and the browser’s key belong to the installation they serve; neither talks to the access service.

The Ask for access button. When the answer is no, the panel’s one button opens Licensor’s request page (https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/request.html) in a new tab with your account name in the page’s address, so the form is filled in for you. As with any page you open, your browser’s history and the web host’s ordinary server logs may record that address.

Access requests. If you ask for access on the request page (a web page, not the extension), the request form records what you enter: your account name, your name, your institutional e-mail, the Google account at which you want the invitation to Beethoven’s private listing on the Chrome Web Store, what you will use Beethoven for, your CV if you attach one (PDF or Word, 5 MB at most), and the time; it also tells the service that it is Beethoven’s request page, which Licensor’s notice of the request shows. That notice is an e-mail to Licensor carrying those items, with a link to the CV that works for 14 days instead of the CV itself. When mailbox confirmation is on (the request page says so after you send), the service first e-mails a link to your university mailbox and passes the request on when you open it, and records the time you did; otherwise the notice says that the mailbox was not confirmed. If you are approved for Beethoven, Licensor adds that Google account to the Google Group whose members may open the private listing; Google then holds it as a member of that group, under Google’s own terms.

Your access record. Licensor’s records hold the approval and withdrawal decisions about your account (an approval is for Beethoven, or for membership of Licensor’s lab only), with the name and e-mail you gave when you asked, their dates, the installation your approval is bound to, and the check record above. Licensor does not publish the list of approved accounts: the access service answers about one account at a time. The same approved list serves Licensor’s other product, an extension for VS Code, so one approval covers both.

A notice under the agreement, if you send one: what you write in it, kept with your access record.

What is never collected

Stated in the negative because reviewers read for what is absent: the extension does not collect command text, file paths, prompt content, job output, portal cookies or tokens, your portal password, the cluster password and verification code you type into its sign-in sheet (it sends them to your cluster and keeps nothing of them), the code you paste to sign in to Claude, anything the portal’s terminal page shows, the key the portal path’s one-time step makes, the private half of the browser’s key (it never leaves your browser), browsing activity, or anything from claude.ai or any Anthropic page. The Bridge collects nothing: it carries the encrypted connection and keeps no record of it. It reads no hardware address, serial number or other identifier from your device and derives none from it: the one identifier of the installation is the random number described above. It sends Licensor no error or crash reports, no usage data and no activation request; the approval check above is the only thing it sends about you. It has no site permission on claude.ai, claude.com or anthropic.com and never asks for one, requests no activeTab, cookies, tabs, webRequest, debugger, identity or clipboardRead permission, uses its nativeMessaging permission only to talk to the Bridge (Chrome lets it reach only a program that registered itself for this extension, and only once you installed one), is granted no website when it is installed (it asks for your portal’s one website when you press Agree and continue, Use this portal or Change under Settings), and runs no code fetched from anywhere.

How Licensor uses and keeps it

A CV attached to a request is deleted twelve months after Licensor decides on the request (twelve months after the request, if no decision is made), or at once if the request is refused or the approval withdrawn. The other access records, including the check record and the installation record, are kept for the life of your access and six years after, to prove the agreement and for accounting and disputes. Nothing is sold or used for advertising. The web host that serves the two daily files sees the requests any web server sees and nothing more. Processors acting for Licensor (hosting; the access service; the e-mail service that carries its notices) see only what they need to run the service. Your cluster password and verification code reach neither Licensor nor any processor of Licensor’s: the extension uses them only to sign you in to your own cluster, when you ask it to, and keeps nothing of them. Licensor’s use of data complies with the Chrome Web Store’s Limited Use requirements.

Security and breaches

Licensor keeps reasonable security measures for the systems that hold access records, and will notify you as Michigan law (MCL 445.72) requires if a breach affects your personal information held by Licensor.

Your choices and rights

Remove the site permission or uninstall the extension at any time; turn the passkey protection of the browser’s key on or off in Settings; use Forget this computer to delete the browser’s key and remove its line from your cluster (or remove the line with hpcworker browser-key remove on the cluster); remove the Bridge (on Windows from Settings, Apps; on a Mac or on Linux, and for a Bridge installed from a zip file with Beethoven 14.0.0 or earlier, with its uninstaller); remove the key of the portal path’s one-time step from your cluster account with hpcworker login-setup --remove; ask Licensor to move your approval to another installation, or for a copy or deletion of your access records (deletion of your access record ends your approval and with it the license). Michigan residents and residents of other states may have further rights under their state’s laws; Licensor honours requests it is obliged to honour and answers others where it reasonably can. Beethoven is offered in the United States.

Children

Beethoven is for adults, or minors with a parent’s or guardian’s consent (LICENSE.txt section 21).

Changes

A new version of this statement ships with the Beethoven version it applies to and is shown for acceptance when it changes materially.

Version 11 (2026-10-04, Beethoven 15.0.0): on Windows and on a Mac the Bridge is now a compiled program of Licensor’s, offered from inside the extension as a signed installer that installs into your own account without administrator rights: on Windows a Windows Installer file signed by Licensor, removed from Settings, Apps; on a Mac an installer package signed by Licensor and notarized by Apple, removed with the uninstaller beside the Bridge. On Linux the Bridge is the script it was. A Bridge installed from a zip file with an earlier version keeps working until you remove it with the uninstaller beside it. When you open a signed installer, your system may check its signature with Apple or Microsoft; that is your system’s own behaviour and tells Licensor nothing. The Bridge does what it did: it reaches only your cluster’s ssh port, carries the encrypted connection and keeps nothing. Nothing new reaches Licensor.

Version 10 (2026-10-02, Beethoven 12.0.0): the extension now tries the ssh path first: an ssh connection to your cluster’s login node, with no VPN, carried by the Bridge, a small helper program that ships inside the extension and that you install once on your computer, without administrator rights; it reaches only your cluster’s ssh port and keeps nothing. The first time, you sign in on the extension’s own sign-in sheet with your account name, password and verification code, which go only to your cluster, inside the encrypted connection, and are never stored; the extension then keeps a key in your browser that no script can copy out, and adds one restricted line to your cluster account that lets that key run only a short list of commands and never sign a worker in to Claude. Protecting that key with a passkey (Windows Hello or Touch ID) is optional and off unless you turn it on. Forget this computer removes the key and the line. Where your cluster has no verification code for you, the extension shows how to set one up yourself, on a computer or on your phone, with QR codes drawn on your device. A relay is not used unless your university’s site profile names one, and this statement would name it first; the pilot app is given only to a student who asks. Without the Bridge the extension works through your portal, as before. The approval check is unchanged and is sent only after your cluster accepts your sign-in. Nothing new reaches Licensor.

Version 9 (2026-10-01, Beethoven 11.0.0): the agreement is accepted on a welcome page with one box and one button, with no typed name; the acceptance record now holds the summary and the sentence shown, whether you opened, scrolled to the end of, saved or printed the full text, and, once your portal first shows it, your account name. The extension now reaches your portal from its own background, on the sign-in your browser keeps, and opens a portal tab only for you to sign in, closing it afterwards, or, on a portal that does not share its sign-in, in the background for one action; after you agree, and before you sign in, it checks whether your portal answers, with requests that carry no sign-in. One command starts your worker and, when needed, the Claude sign-in, and writes your Remote Control answer; the framework keeps a plain-words progress log for each worker. Where the portal’s shell asks for a password, a one-time step makes a key in your cluster account that only your institution’s Open OnDemand server can use; you type your password into the portal’s own terminal page, and the extension never sees it and keeps nothing about the key. New on your device: your worker’s last known state and link, how the extension reaches your portal, your last five waits, the tour and the one-time tips seen, an activity list for Show log, the tabs it opened itself, and your appearance choice; the note of the tab the toolbar button was clicked from is gone, with the activeTab permission. The QR code for your phone and the tour are drawn on your device. The statement now names what the access service keeps from the checks (how many, and the reason given with a no), the reviewers’ mock account, and that the list of approved accounts is not published, and says “no site permission on claude.ai” where it said “no access”. Nothing new reaches Licensor.

Version 8 (2026-09-30, Beethoven 8.0.0): the extension no longer carries the framework’s scripts and never copies them into your account. It works only with the one shared copy your university’s lab keeps on the cluster; where there is none, or your account cannot use it, it says so and names whom to ask, and uploads nothing. The note of the install it ran no longer counts uploaded files. One approved account, one installation: the approval check now also sends the random installation identifier the extension already kept, and the service binds an approval to the first installation that asks, refuses any other until Licensor moves the approval, refuses that installation for any other account, and keeps what One approved account, one installation says. Beethoven is offered only through a private listing on the Chrome Web Store. The request page now also asks for the Google account that receives the invitation to that listing, takes an optional CV (deleted twelve months after the decision), and may ask you to confirm your university mailbox.

Version 7 (2026-09-29, Beethoven 7.0.0): the product has a new name, Beethoven, and new addresses. Its pages, the support page and the request page are under https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/; the two daily files are https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/services.json and https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/killlist.json; the access service answers at https://beethoven-access.openspineconsortium.workers.dev, a second name for the same service, which keeps the same records. The request page now also tells the service which product’s page a request was sent from. Nothing about the data changed: the extension keeps, sends and receives the same items as under version 6, and Licensor records the same.

Version 6 (2026-09-29, extension 5.0.0): where your institution’s lab keeps one shared, read-only copy of the cluster-side scripts, the extension no longer copies them into your account; it writes a small launcher, a one-line marker naming the lab’s copy and your profile, and reads that copy’s version file through your portal. Nothing new leaves your device and nothing new reaches Licensor. The install note the extension keeps is also written when you press “Set up the cluster again” under Details.

Version 5 (2026-09-29, extension 4.0.0): there are no license keys any more, and nothing to type or paste. Your own sign-in to your portal identifies you, by the account name the portal’s dashboard shows; the extension confirms with Licensor’s access service that this account is approved when you connect, when you click the icon and about once a day, and that check is now the one request that carries anything about you (the account name, the portal’s hostname, the product and its version; Licensor records those with the time, a salted hash of the network address and the answer). The daily list withdraws versions only; the extension also reads a daily services file for the service’s address. The table rows for the key and the identifier are replaced by the account name and the last answer; the Ask for access button, which carries your account name in the page’s address, is named. Nothing else changed.

Version 4 (2026-09-29): the statement now describes the software as built. Earlier versions described an activation request and optional error reports; the extension has neither (there is no code for them and no address to send them to), so the sections that described them are removed and the section “What Licensor receives” names the one request the extension makes to Licensor, the daily withdrawn-keys list. The record Licensor keeps when it issues a key is named for what it is. Nothing new leaves your device; less was ever leaving it than the earlier text said.

Version 3 (2026-09-29): the extension now starts the Claude sign-in sitting for you and takes the pasted code in its own panel (the section “What happens when you sign in to Claude” is new); your statement about a worker’s workspace is kept per workspace in the browser instead of per browser session, and now includes your answer to Claude Code’s Remote Control question, which the extension records in one marker file in your cluster account; the notes the extension keeps so its automatic steps do not repeat (the last sign-in it saw, the links it opened, the check job it submitted, the install it ran) are listed; the session-state row names everything the run record holds, including the last 4,000 characters of the worker’s own log; the preference “open claude.ai when my worker connects” is added; the audit-log row says what it never holds. Nothing new leaves your device or your accounts.

Version 2 (2026-09-29): added the checklist tick, the start-by-itself preference and the session’s claude.ai link to the table of what stays in your browser, and named the withdrawn-keys copy and the installation identifier that were already kept there. Nothing new leaves your device.

Beethoven's use of information received from your browser complies with the Chrome Web Store User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements.
